doc.title: Jack DeJohnette — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Von Freeman, Fathers and Sons, Fred Anderson and the Chicago connection
summary: Playing with Von Freeman at the Jazz Showcase and on Fathers and Sons, and memories of Fred Anderson.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: One more project if I may and that’s a project with Von Freeman.
Right, I bring this up only because Von Freeman also received the NEA Jazz Master, and we’re trying to capture his oral history as well but he’s been ill.
We’re hoping that he’s going to recover and be OK. But that relationship must have been formed when you were in Chicago.

Yeah, it was and it was formed again when I came back to Chicago and played Joe Segal’s Jazz Showcase. I had a band that was made up of Larry Gray on bass, a very fantastic bassist who plays with Ramsey. Larry Gray, the legendary Jodie Christian on piano, and Ira Sullivan. I did a week with Von Freeman with my quintet, which I have some documents of. That was great, playing with Von on a nightly basis. He had Ira and Jodie. It was fantastic. Anyway, the Fathers And Sons idea was for Columbia Records because of Wynton and Ellis on the other side. So, it was this half record there that was done. So it was great to play with…
…Kenny Barron, Chico and Von, and Cecil McBee on bass. I just wanted to bring that up again because it goes back to the Chicago connection.
He wasn’t on the date. I don’t recall hearing a trumpet in that group.
Speaking of saxophonists who rarely left Chicago, Fred Anderson.
Oh yeah! I knew Fred. Fred Anderson and Billy Brimfield. Both of those guys… I think I heard them both. Billy I played with a little bit. Is Billy still around?
I don’t know, but Fred passed recently.
Yeah, because he had The Velvet Lounge.

I don’t know since he died. I remember the last time I saw him, with Leonard Brown by the way, was about four or five years ago and he was getting ready to move… I don’t know. I know he had moved in it and established, but I don’t know if it’s going to this day without him.

OK, (it was) always a pleasure to play with Von, you never knew what he was going to play. He was a beautiful ballad player like Gene Ammons, and that he could play ballads. He could play as lyrical as you want, and go as out as you want to go. He’s one of those very special legends and I’m really happy to have the association… To play with him and glad to share this NEA award along with him.
